If you only remember one thing: the A I industry is learning that more A I is not the same as more value, and everyone, from Microsoft to Anthropic, is pulling back to fix the basics.

Number one. A I products. From your Rundown. Microsoft's head of Copilot, Jacob Andreou, says the company removed Copilot from several Windows apps, because those entry points brought traffic but little value. Fewer entry points, more usage per person. He also says no single lab wins at everything anymore. Microsoft's new Auto mode picks the best model for each task. Why it matters: the winner is now the product built around the model, not the model alone.

Number two. China's A I money race. From your China A I Weekly Digest. DeepSeek is raising at least twelve billion dollars, with Tencent backing it. Reports say it could reach fifteen billion. That would be one of the largest private rounds ever for an A I company. Manus raised over five hundred million dollars after splitting from Meta. And Kling, the video A I from Kuaishou, is picking banks for an I P O of more than one billion dollars. Also, the U S issued its first fine under its outbound investment rules, over a Chinese robotics A I deal. Why it matters: capital and export rules are now the real battleground between the U S and China.

Number three. A I safety and policy. From TechCrunch. Microsoft C E O Satya Nadella says A I models need an emergency brake. And Anthropic says it can't reliably control its A I agents, so it is cutting its internal tests off from the live internet. Why it matters: even the labs are admitting that agents are hard to control, which strengthens the case for rules.

Number four. Data centers. TechCrunch asks whether A I companies can win over local opponents of data centers by dropping the secrecy agreements on those deals. Why it matters: community trust, not just chips and power, may decide where A I gets built.

Also quick. Apple is hiring the team behind a personalized podcast startup called Huxe. And a new A I model maker called Jev was valued at seven point five billion dollars, just weeks after launch.

Also in your Reads. The New Yorker has David Remnick on the coming midterms. Tech Policy Press looks at kids learning to code, drone wars, and new books on technology.

Good news close. Voice A I companies say their big breakout moment hasn't arrived yet, which means there is still plenty of room for tools that help people. And open models keep spreading, with Alibaba arguing open source is Europe's best chance in A I.

The thread today: A I is growing up. Less hype, more control, and bigger bets on who gets to build it. That's your briefing. Have a great Monday.
